title: The lifespan of the Tathagata (Kern ch. 15)
hook: the Buddha reveals he awakened countless ages ago and is always present

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ground split open and bodhisattvas nobody knew rose up, all taught by the Buddha himself. Your line: they rose from the earth. And Maitreya was left asking how. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

A prince of the Sakya clan leaves his palace. He sits down near the town of Gaya, under a tree, and there he wakes up. Not so long ago. That's what makes yesterday's crowd from under the earth impossible: how could a man who woke up not long ago have taught so many? Before he answers, the Buddha does something unusual. He says, more than once: trust what I'm about to tell you. And more than once, the whole assembly asks him to go on. A teacher who asks for trust before speaking is about to say something hard to hear. Today: the lifespan of the Tathagata.
screen: `A PRINCE, A TREE, NEAR GAYA.` → `NOT SO LONG AGO?` → `TRUST WHAT I TELL YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the story the world believes. The Buddha says it himself: gods and people all think that Shakyamuni left the palace of the Sakyas and woke up at the seat near Gaya. Second, what he actually says. It's been ages beyond reckoning since I awoke. Then he reaches for a picture like the one in chapter seven, only larger. Grind whole worlds into dust, and drop a grain each time you pass a vast stretch of worlds, until the dust runs out. Now grind every world you passed, landed on or not, into dust too, and let each grain be an age. More time than that, he says, has gone by since he woke. And all through it, he says, I've been here in this world, teaching. Third, why he seems to leave. If people could see him every day, he says, the ones with little root of goodness would grow lazy. They'd take him for granted. They'd stop feeling that meeting a Buddha is rare. So he appears to pass into nirvana. He calls it a skillful means. Tomorrow he tells a story about a doctor to explain it. Fourth, the verses. In the chapter's verses, the Buddha says he is always here, on the mountain called Vulture Peak, teaching. People with confused eyes don't see him, even when he's near. When people long to see him with their whole heart, he and his assembly appear. Some schools treat this chapter as the heart of the whole sutra. What the chapter claims is simple and enormous: the Buddha hasn't left. In its words, he is always here, and people just don't always see him.
screen: `THE STORY THE WORLD BELIEVES.` · `AGES BEYOND DUST.` · `WHY HE SEEMS TO LEAVE.` · `ALWAYS HERE, ON VULTURE PEAK.` · then, large: `ALWAYS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: feel present to someone far. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind one person who is far from you: in another city, another country, or, if it feels right, someone no longer living. Let their face come clear. Notice what of them you still carry: a phrase they use, the way they laugh, a thing they taught you. Rest with them nearby for a few breaths, as close as the breath. Then let the picture soften, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The lifespan of the Tathagata. Awake for ages beyond counting, teaching all along, seeming to pass away only so people won't take him for granted. Today's word.
screen: `THE LIFESPAN OF THE TATHAGATA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: always here. Today, send one message to someone far away, just to say you're still here too. Day one thousand one hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter is often recited, especially its verses, and some schools, including Tiantai and Nichiren traditions, treat it as the heart of the sutra.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. you could stay visible forever, but people who see you every day start taking you for granted. what do you do?
options: stay visible: people will figure it out.
appear to pass away, so they'll value the teaching.
fork.reveal: he appears to pass into nirvana, though he's always here. the chapter calls it a skillful means, and tomorrow's story explains it.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the Buddha's name for himself, often explained as the one thus gone, or thus come.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha lived one lifetime and then he was gone.
what it means: in this chapter he says he woke ages beyond counting ago, has been teaching all along, and only seems to pass away.
what a scholar hears: some schools, Tiantai and Nichiren among them, treat this chapter as the heart of the Lotus, the place where the Buddha's real lifespan is shown.

notes: Chapter paraphrased from Kern (1884) ch. 15, not quoted (wording unverified). Check: the repeated request to believe (three times in some versions, with the assembly's request repeated; left vague as 'more than once'); 'the world thinks he left the Sakya palace and awoke near Gaya'; the dust simile (summarized loosely); teaching all along in this and other worlds; apparent nirvana as skillful means so beings of little merit won't grow lax.

Verses: 'always here on Vulture Peak (Grdhrakuta), unseen by those with confused minds, appearing when beings long to see him' paraphrased; confirm these verses are in the Sanskrit/Kern as well as Kumarajiva.
'Some schools treat this chapter as the heart of the sutra' (Tiantai, Nichiren) is a general reception claim; confirm.
Practice invites thinking of someone no longer living 'if it feels right'; check it sits comfortably with the chapter.
Original: तथागत (tathāgata) with the usual 'thus gone / thus come' explanation, attributed as 'often explained as'.

Editor: hook no longer opens and the teach no longer repeats 'the story the world believes' twice; dust picture shortened and tied to chapter seven (day 1160 used it); dropped the 'loving trick ... since the burning house' link (tomorrow makes that link); the closing 'he's always here' is now framed as the chapter's claim, not the narrator's; practice no longer tells the listener what is in them.
